job.style: a short story with Indian characters in everyday life

passage: Rohan and Meera were helping their grandfather fix an old torch in their village home. Rohan noticed the torch had two cells inside. He tried to place them both with their metal caps facing the same direction, but Grandfather gently corrected him, explaining that the positive terminal of one cell must touch the negative terminal of the other for the circuit to work. Meera asked if the electricity gets used up inside the bulb, making the current weaker when it returns to the battery. Grandfather smiled and explained that current is a continuous flow; the bulb simply converts electrical energy into light and heat, but the same amount of current returns to the battery. He then showed them the bulb, pointing out that one wire connects to the base tip and another to the metal casing on the side. He warned them that a circuit is only complete when both these distinct points are connected to the battery. Finally, he tested a piece of dry wood and a plastic scale, noting that while some materials like metals are conductors, many non-metals are insulators, though some special materials can conduct under specific conditions. He reminded them that air is generally an insulator, preventing electricity from jumping across gaps.

items.evidence: He tried to place them both with their metal caps facing the same direction, but Grandfather gently corrected him, explaining that the positive terminal of one cell must touch the negative terminal of the other for the circuit to work.
items.q: Rohan puts both cells in the torch with metal caps facing the same way. What happens?
options: The bulb stays off; cells are joined wrongly
The bulb glows; cell direction does not matter
The bulb glows dimly; only one cell works
The bulb glows brighter; both caps push together
items.explain: The positive end of one cell must touch the negative end of the other, or the circuit fails.

wrong.why: thinks cells work whichever way they face
thinks one cell still works on its own
thinks same-facing cells add their push

items.evidence: Grandfather smiled and explained that current is a continuous flow; the bulb simply converts electrical energy into light and heat, but the same amount of current returns to the battery.
items.q: How does the current returning to the battery compare with the current leaving it?
options: It is exactly the same amount
It is less, as the bulb uses some
It is zero, as it stops at the bulb
It is more, as the bulb adds heat
items.explain: Current is a continuous flow; the bulb changes energy into light and heat, but no current is lost.

wrong.why: thinks the bulb uses up current
thinks current flows to the bulb and stops
reverses the idea of light and heat being made

items.evidence: He then showed them the bulb, pointing out that one wire connects to the base tip and another to the metal casing on the side.
items.q: Meera's bulb has one wire on its base tip and one on its glass. What must she change?
options: Move the glass wire to the side metal casing
Move both wires onto the base tip
Press the glass wire more firmly on the bulb
Add one more cell to fill it with electricity
items.explain: A bulb has two contact points: the base tip and the metal casing on the side.

wrong.why: thinks the bulb has only one terminal at the tip
thinks touching the bulb anywhere closes the circuit
thinks a battery just pours out stored electricity

items.evidence: Finally, he tested a piece of dry wood and a plastic scale, noting that while some materials like metals are conductors, many non-metals are insulators, though some special materials can conduct under specific conditions.
items.q: Meera says no non-metal can ever conduct. How would Grandfather correct her?
options: Some special materials conduct under certain conditions
All non-metals conduct if they are dry
Metals and non-metals conduct equally well
Only air conducts, as it carries lightning
items.explain: Many non-metals are insulators, but some special materials can conduct under specific conditions.

wrong.why: reverses the dry wood test result
ignores the difference between conductors and insulators
thinks air conducts because of lightning

items.evidence: He reminded them that air is generally an insulator, preventing electricity from jumping across gaps.
items.q: A wire in the torch breaks, leaving a tiny air gap. Why does the bulb go off?
options: Air does not let current jump the gap
Air carries current but stores it in the gap
Air conducts, but only during lightning storms
Air pushes the current back into the battery
items.explain: Air is generally an insulator, so electricity cannot jump across the gap and the circuit breaks.

wrong.why: thinks an open gap stores electricity
thinks air is a conductor because of lightning
imagines current bouncing back at a gap
